Data centers do what any industry would to continue operations during a power outage: Quickly pivot to their own emergency energy. As reported in several media outlets, a 10-minute grid outage in late July of this year on the East Coast caused data centers to hop off the main grid and switch over to their own backup power. The disconnection by the data centers was enough to cause flickering lights across half the U.S.
COMMENTARY
This time, all we experienced were flickers. With more data centers coming online across the country connecting to our grids, if another outage prompted all of them to switch to their own power sources all at once, next time we could have full-on blackouts. This is why grid utilities, data centers, and regulators are all looking at the next steps to prevent something like this from happening again. Behind-the-meter solutions have been a fix for long interconnection queues, but most data centers will need to connect to the power grid at some point. These large-load interconnections have introduced new grid-code requirements and pushed power stability and reliability to the brink.
In response, at the federal level, FERC is considering broader reforms for large-load interconnections, while NERC has been directed to develop mandatory reliability standards for computational loads. But it’s Texas, through ERCOT, that is furthest along with specific requirements. ERCOT’s large-load framework applies to facilities of 75 MW or more, and its proposed large electronic load ride-through rules would require qualifying data centers to remain connected through defined voltage and frequency disturbances rather than immediately dropping from the grid. But what do these evolving regulations and standards mean for reliability and consistency of power?
There is a simple, yet effective solution to large-load interconnection challenges—a reconfiguration of the typical uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system to support stability on both sides of the device.
By reconfiguring the UPS system (Figure 1) to provide stability from both the grid- and load-side converters and pairing it with a continuously running battery, we could essentially prevent fluctuations in power consumption from the grid. This configuration allows for much better control of power and only requires the typical control functions used in converters.
1. Proposed UPS configuration: A double conversion type UPS with a grid-side converter, load-side converter, and battery DC/DC converter. Source: Ramboll
Turning UPS Systems Into Grid-Stabilizing Devices
In the typical configuration, a UPS battery kicks in as the grid voltage drops, and the grid-side power consumption cuts off. Then when the grid voltage recovers, the battery transfers the load back to the grid with a delay. However, the proposed reconfiguration, when paired with a continuously running battery, would eliminate the need for consumption cut off and allow for smooth power and ride-through during times of disruption.
At its core, the reconfiguration is a double conversion type UPS with a grid-side converter, load-side converter, and battery DC/DC converter. The battery sits in the middle of the system and continuous helps to balance power by either supplying or absorbing excess power. The battery essentially acts as a buffer between the grid and the data center.
On the data center side (the load side), the converter manages voltage and frequency regulation, ensuring that the facility receives steady, regulated power to protect the IT equipment from the effects of fluctuations. Meanwhile, the grid-side converter controls the flow of power, helping to smooth demand changes and support stability.
With further modifications, this system could be used for grid-support functions, acting as a stabilizing power source that sets the rhythm for the electrical system. If necessary, grid forming control functionalities can be introduced for the grid side converters to reinforce the support further. With the right controls, the proposed configuration could help manage voltage, reactive power, frequency response, ride-through during grid faults, harmonics, and electrical oscillations.
Testing the Concept Under Real-World Load Swings
To demonstrate viability, my colleagues at Ramboll and I developed a test system featuring an AI data center training load profile with a peak load of about 100 MW. The UPS model had a total rated power of 120 MW, supported by a battery with a total capacity of 120 MWh (one hour of rated power supply). The grid-side converter operated in “grid-following” mode, where the battery follows the grid’s existing voltage and frequency, with both active power control and reactive power control (Q = 0).
The active power consumption at the load-side and grid-side converters are shown in Figure 2.
The test showed that the UPS absorbed the major load fluctuations and high-frequency ripples and kept the power draw smooth and gradual. For the small simulation time window, the state of charge (SOC) of the battery was kept almost at 90%. If necessary, the grid-side power can be kept even smoother by allowing a larger energy fluctuation in the battery.
Figure 3 shows the system performance for a 100-millisecond, three-phase-to-ground fault at the interconnection point. The results showed no significant interruption on the load side, indicating that the proposed configuration maintained stable power throughout the disturbance. The grid side converter recovered well after the disturbance; similar to a well-designed BESS system.
Supporting Reliable Growth
As large data centers continue to reshape power demand, reliability will depend on solutions that support both facility operations and grid stability. This reconfigured UPS system, paired with a continuously running battery, can help smooth rapid load changes, maintain power through grid disturbances, and support emerging ride-through requirements without requiring a fundamentally new system architecture. For utilities, regulators, and data center operators, this practical, converter-based configuration offers a pathway to keep critical digital infrastructure online while reducing stress on the broader power system.
— Dr. Chandana Karawita is a senior technical manager for System Studies & System Analysis at Ramboll , a global architecture, engineering, and consultancy company founded in Denmark in 1945 with the mission to create sustainable societies where people and nature flourish.

2026 Paris Motor Show • Ford Rolls Out the Ranger MS-RT Champion Edition: You Can Choose Any Color As Long as It Is Black
Evotrex-PG5 Is Almost Here: The First RV Trailer Capable of Generating Its Own Power
15 photos
Photo: Evotrex
Set your alarm clocks and mark your calendars because we're on step closer to seeing the first-ever production-intent unit of the trailer described as the first-ever RV trailer capable of generating its own power. Evotrex-PG5, the trailer in question, is en route to its big public debut.
The name Evotrex will probably ring familiar to the RV enthusiasts. They're one of the handful of RV startups making headlines over the past couple of years and one of the fewer to show real promise in terms of delivering the product they're promising. As of last week, they're even more worthy of attention.
That's when Evotrex announced the digital debut of the Evotrex-PG5 travel trailer , the production-intent version, for January 5, 2027, followed by the physical debut of the same product a few days later, at the 2027 edition of CES, taking place in Las Vegas.
This double debut confirms that PG5, described by trade outlets as a true pioneer in the premium towable sector, is on track for the first customer deliveries for mid 2027. Limited production will kick off later next year, with the first units going out to the first reservation holders.
Photo: Evotrex "Something capable is approaching" This is how Evotrex is teasing the upcoming debut. It won't be the first time media and potential customers are laying eyes on the PG5, since it made its debut in prototype form at this year's CES, but it will be the first time they're seeing the production-intent version of it. Unlike the prototype, this one will be closer to the units that will be heading out to customers next summer.
It will also integrate new features and upgrades based on feedback from the RV community, as Alex Xiao, founder and CEO of Evotrex, points out.
Photo: Evotrex "January 5 will mark an important step forward for Evotrex," he says in a statement. "We have spent this development phase listening to our community, testing in real-world conditions and refining the details that matter most."
He doesn't get into specifics, most likely because the specifics will be revealed in January. The full list of specs is also expected to be revealed then, so we'll know more about construction method and materials, weights, and exact dimensions for both the trailer and the holding tanks.
With the announcement regarding the upcoming debut comes the launch of the Evotrex Rewards program, which will see referrals rewarded with points that can be used for purchase in the Evotrex online store or for the acquisition of a new PG5 trailer.
Photo: Evotrex So, what's the fuss with this travel trailer? These technicalities aside, one thing that won't change about the PG5 between prototype stage and production-intent version is the thing that makes it so special : the fact that it's capable of generating its own power. This 28-foot (8.5-meter) trailer is fully electric, but with a different approach to self-sufficiency than the majority of fully electric options available right now or in the making.
It comes with 1.5kW of solar on the roof and a massive 43kWh lithium battery, but it doesn't rely solely on energy from the sun for extended off-grid stays. That same integrated system features a 75kW automotive-grade generator with its own fuel tank that will charge the battery on the go or when there's limited exposure.
The system comes with V2V DC fast charging so you will be able to charge the towing vehicle from the battery or even to use it as a backup power source for the home, in case of a power shortage.
Photo: Evotrex The PG5 features smart power management, an Off-Grid Calculator for real-time estimates based on available resources, and an onboard electric motor that will allow parking and remote maneuvering on the app or by remote. A TowSync function will provide towing assistance on the road, reducing the load on the towing vehicle.
Other figures revealed earlier this year with the prototype but not confirmed by Evotrex is a gross weight of about 9,900 lbs (4,490 kg) and 43 square feet (4 square meters) for the drop-down patio that will also function as a ramp, allowing you to load smaller toys and gear into the space of the dinette.
The trailer rides on a tandem axle with 33-inch offroad tires and features a zero-wood construction and interior. Metal, fiberglass, and composites will be used heavily for both, based on how the first functional prototype looked.
Photo: Evotrex In terms of layout, the PG5 has the main bedroom at the front, the lounge slash dining space slash garage at the rear, and the kitchen and bathroom in the middle. This is a four-person RV that will work wonderfully as a complete option for a couple's RV , with premium appliances, maximum comfort, and surprisingly sophisticated styling.
Evotrex will offer several trims for the same model, the PG5, with prices starting at $119,990 for the most basic one and $159,990 for the Premium configuration, which was previously called Atlas.
The Atlas prototype is shown in the second video below.

2026 Paris Motor Show • Hyundai Tucson N Line Steals the Spotlight in Paris, but It's All Show and No Go
Elon Musk Wants Tesla To Double Its Production Capacity by 2030, Does This Even Make Sense?
7 photos
Photo: Tesla
For years, Elon Musk insisted that Tesla is no longer a carmaker, but an AI and robotics company. This coincided with EV sales plummeting in 2024 and 2025, which prompted Musk to pivot Tesla's strategy. However, Tesla sales miraculously rebounded in 2026, and not only is Tesla a carmaker again, but Musk wants to double production capacity. What gives?
Tesla held its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, after releasing some mixed financial results that split investors and analysts. Unlike the shareholder deck, the conference allowed Tesla to present a clearer picture of its operations. As is often the case, Tesla tried to dazzle investors with rosy prospects, and in many ways, it succeeded.
However, another part of the call raised serious questions: Elon Musk announced that Tesla aims to double production capacity to 5 million vehicles per year. And he wants to do it fast, by the end of 2030. This marks an abrupt change of direction after years of turning his back on vehicle manufacturing. We've read and heard the "Tesla is not a carmaker" mantra many times, but now things appear to move in the opposite direction.
From sustainable transport and energy to "amazing abundance" Over the past three years, Tesla went from plans to save the Earth with sustainable transportation, solar panels, and energy storage, to a fuzzy concept of "amazing abundance" that not even Musk can explain what it means exactly. Since then, the affordable Gen-3 compact EV was canceled, and the Model S and Model X were retired without successors. Instead, Tesla insisted that autonomous vehicles and robots are the company's future.
Many mocked Tesla's new ethos as a taxi company, but we have to give it credit for its Robotaxi service. What started as a pilot has since been expanded into a dependable transportation service in Austin using unsupervised vehicles. The Cybercab, which recently started volume production, has increased its presence, while safety records have proved that its autonomous driving system is at least as safe as Waymo's.
Meanwhile, nobody believed that Tesla would put much effort into expanding its EV portfolio. It never was the kind of traditional carmaker committed to regularly overhauling its model lineup. The Model 3 and Model Y were the only ones to receive meaningful updates, and that's not counting the stripped-down Standard variants. With the Cybertruck program in shambles and no new vehicle plans in the pipeline, Tesla looked set to abandon its automotive plans.
And don't even get me started on the Roadster, which was merely a PR stunt with little practical value. Even if Tesla finds a way and a time to start building it, it will be a small series model for collectors rather than a new vehicle line. However, there's some merit in the Roadster, beyond its qualities as a driver's car. Specifically, it's the only thing that made Musk reconsider cars.
From no new models to doubling the vehicle production There might be no connection between the Roadster's epic demo and the decision to double Tesla vehicle production capacity. However, given that Musk made the announcement roughly one week after watching the Roadster flying and rolling in the air, I believe that the October 15 event influenced him somehow. Maybe (he might have thought) cars can be cool after all.
Regardless of what made Musk change his mind , we now have this new announcement to make sense of. "We've been laying the groundwork for a lot more manufacturing capacity," Musk told investors at the earnings call. "We're aiming for 5 million vehicles a year by 2030." Now that's indeed a strong statement from a company that didn't want to talk about new car models not long ago.
Tesla already has more production capacity than it can use. According to Tesla's latest data, it can theoretically build 1,5 million Model 3 and Model Y vehicles in Fremont and Shanghai, plus another 750.000 Model Y vehicles across Austin and Berlin. That's a 2.25-million annual capacity for the two popular EVs plus 125,000 Cybertrucks and 125,000 Cybercabs. Tesla Semi accounts for an additional 25,000-unit capacity.
Meanwhile, Tesla sales maxed out at 1.8 million in 2023, and it's not yet clear if it could match that performance in 2026. Why does Tesla need twice the production capacity, and why so fast, by the end of 2030? Why does Musk expect Tesla to triple its vehicle sales in just four years? Does Musk really think that Cybercab production could reach the 2-million-unit level he promised in 2023? Or does it have other mass-market models in the pipeline that he expects to require a production capacity increase?
Two million Cybercabs or new mass-market models? If we're to consider what Musk told investors during the third-quarter earnings call , he believes that Tesla could've sold more vehicles in the quarter. Musk blamed tight battery supply for not being able to increase production. Certainly, the EV sales boom caused by high fuel prices could hardly be anticipated. It's obvious that Tesla was caught off-guard by the strong demand, especially in China and Europe.
However, going from selling "more" to selling three times as many vehicles is a long stretch. When Tesla launched Cybercab's production, Musk was confident that it could sell 2 million units per year. However, that's almost incomprehensible, considering the lack of customer appeal of a car with no controls and only two seats.
During the call, Musk announced that Tesla would sell the first Cybercab units to customers later this year. However, he also admitted that these customers would be fleet operators, not private owners. Musk also said that the vast majority of Cybercabs would be owned by Tesla, so, again, no private customers. Does Tesla need 2 million new Cybercabs every year for its own operations? That's a question that's worth a lot of money.
The only other possibility is that Tesla reconsidered its previous position and is now working on new vehicle models. If that's true, it could start with the affordable compact EV that shares the unboxed Gen-3 platform with the Cybercab. That would be the easiest and cheapest route to doubling production. Certainly, more new mass-market models would help fill that 5-million annual capacity much faster.

Networking
Workstation
Qotom Q51551UT-Rear 1
With a sea of performance and efficient cores, an Intel iGPU, NPU, six 2.5GbE ports, two SFP+ 10G ports, and two 10Gbase-T ports, the Qotom Q51551UT does a bit of everything. At first, you might think this is a networking box looking at the rear panel. Then you see multiple display outputs and wonder if it is a desktop. Once you install Proxmox VE, it becomes a virtualization platform. While it can do a lot, several caveats make it interesting enough that we also have a video for it, debuting some of our new graphics look.
Today we are looking at a Qotom design that places heavy emphasis on networking: the Qotom Q51551UT. Part of the company’s larger Q31500UT S18 Series, the Q51551UT features eight RJ45 Ethernet jacks, plus a couple more SFP+ ports for good measure. As a result, the mini-PC is well suited to networking-centric workloads that require multiple high-speed Ethernet connections, whether as a software firewall or a more typical edge computer.
Qotom Q51551UT Key Specs
Processor | Intel Core Ultra 5 125H, 4P + 8E + 2LPE (4.5GHz)
Operating System | Pre-Installed: None (As tested: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS)
Memory | 96GB DDR5-5600 (2x48GB SO-DIMM)
System Storage | 128GB SSD (PCIe Gen3 x4, M.2 2242)
PCIe Slots | 1x Headless PCIe x16 (Gen5 x8 Electrical)
GPU | Intel Arc Graphics (Xe-LPG, 7 cores)
PSU | 120W External PSU
Form Factor | Mini-PC
Dimensions | 200 x 200 x 53 mm (7.9 x 7.9 x 2.1 in)
Weight | 1.75 kg (3.9lbs)
Networking | 6x 2.5GbE (RJ45, Intel I226-V) 2x 10GbE (RJ45, Intel X540-AT2) 2x 10GbE (SFP+, Intel X710-BM2)
Color | Silver (Aluminum)
Ports | Front: 1x USB-A 5Gbps, 4x USB-A 480Mbps, 3.5mm Audio Jack, 1x Serial (RJ45) Rear: 2x USB-A 5Gbps, 1x USB-C 5Gbps, 1x DisplayPort 1.4, 1x HDMI 2.0, 6x 2.5GbE (RJ45), 2x 10GbE (RJ45), 2x 10GbE (SFP+)
The Q51551UT is notable because it has no “slow” Ethernet interfaces. Every single port is at least 2.5GbE, while a smaller set of ports (including the SFP+ ports) supports 10GbE. So it is not just a mini-PC with a lot of connectivity. It is a mini-PC with the bandwidth to back it up.
Here is an AliExpress Affiliate link to the unit. Always double-check the options before you buy.
Qotom Q51551UT External Hardware Overview
With this type of system, we typically see two styles: either a fully passive system filled with heatsink fins, or a smaller system that relies on active cooling. Qotom’s Q51551UT falls into the latter category, using a low-profile blower to cool the system. With ventilation on virtually every side except the front, it is a downright airy system.
Starting our brief tour from the front of the system, the Q51551UT looks like a fairly consumer-ish mini-PC at first glance, with a mix of power buttons and I/O ports. Looking a bit more closely, though, we can quickly see the telltale signs that this mini-PC is geared toward the industrial market.
Qotom Q51551UT-Front 1
All told, Qotom has equipped the system with five USB-A ports on the front. Only one of these ports supports high-speed (5Gbps) operation. The rest are USB 2.0 ports (480Mbps), designed to hook up a larger-than-normal number of peripherals. As we will see in a bit, part of this design is also pragmatic, since the rear of the system is consumed by Ethernet ports.
Speaking of networking, the system has an RJ45 jack on the front. But this is not an Ethernet jack. Instead, it is an RJ45-form-factor RS-232 serial port. Next to it are the system status LEDs and a ringed power button.
While Qotom’s promotional material shows the system in multiple orientations, in practice it is meant to sit on its side unless you mount it via a VESA bracket. That is because only the left edge (or rather, bottom edge) has any rubber feet, while the bottom lacks any mechanism to elevate the system and keep its bottom air intake cool.
Qotom Q51551UT-Front Angled 4
Shifting gears to the rear of the system, here we can see the Q51551UT’s true specialization in action: Ethernet ports. Lots of Ethernet ports.
Qotom Q51551UT-Rear 1
With 10 ports in total, the Q51551UT is a networking powerhouse in both the number of connections and the bandwidth available.
Starting from the right side, we have a pair of SFP+ ports driven by an Intel X710-BM2 controller. The Fortville controller is over a decade old, but it has proven to be a reliable networking platform, giving the Q51551UT the option of using either 1GbE or 10GbE modules and an easy way to add optical networking to the system.
Qotom Q51551UT-10G SFP+ Ports 1
To the left, we have the first two RJ45 Ethernet jacks, which are a distinctive red. This indicates they are 10GbE jacks, powered by Intel’s X540-AT2 (Twinville) controller. This dual-port 10GbE controller gives the system a pair of ports for copper 10GbE connectivity. Selecting the X540 controller is a bit puzzling, as it is a 16-year-old (and long-discontinued) Intel design that predates the newer NBASE-T standard, meaning these ports don’t support the intermediate 2.5Gbps or 5Gbps speeds. For carefully planned applications, this should not be an issue, but it is an atypically inflexible design for a modern mini-PC.
Qotom Q51551UT-10G LAN Ports 1
That said, if you need 2.5Gbps connectivity, Qotom has you covered with the remaining Ethernet ports. To the left of the 10GbE jacks are six additional RJ45 Ethernet jacks, all powered by Intel’s I226-V controller. Using the company’s modern mainstream 2.5GbE controller, these ports can run at up to 2.5Gbps or any speed below that, and they provide most of the mini-PC’s network connectivity.
Qotom Q51551UT-2.5G LAN Ports 1
However, Qotom’s specification sheet indicates that the RJ45 jacks are wired so there is not enough bandwidth to run every NIC at full speed at once. Each of the 2.5GbE ports has a Gen2 x1 connection, and two of the 10G ports share 12Gbps of upstream bandwidth, while the other two 10G ports have sufficient PCIe connectivity. We will get into that later in our review.
Aside from network connectivity, the rest of the rear I/O space on the Q51551UT is for USB and display connectivity. Here is the system’s sole USB-C port, which runs at just 5Gbps. At the far edge are two additional 5Gbps USB-A ports.
Qotom Q51551UT-Display Port 1
